dedupe_keys.name: environmental justice and systems analysis for air quality planning in the port of oakland

description: This study by Fiona Greer, Ahmad Bin Thaneya and Arpad Horvath of the University of California, Berkeley, published in Environmental Science & Technology in 2024, brings environmental justice and life-cycle thinking into air quality planning for the Port of Oakland, a multimodal marine port next to the historically marginalised West Oakland community. Coverage: fine particulate matter (PM2.5) exposure and monetised damages from operating and maintaining the port, over an exposure domain covering the whole San Francisco Bay Area and its more than 7.5 million people, from an inventory of more than 14 sources including supply chain emissions from material production, delivery and fuel production. Ocean-going container ships dominate intake; supply chain sources give 3.5% to 7.5%. Damages are USD 100 to 270 million a year, and Black residents and the lowest income quintile are 2.2 and 1.9 times more disproportionately exposed. Format and access: an open article with full text on PubMed Central. Licence and cost: free under CC BY 4.0. Caveats: damage ranges depend on concentration-response relationships, hazard ratios and resurfacing assumptions. The source shares and mitigation results (3.5% from electrified trucking against 8.7% to 55% from vessel and harbour craft measures) can rank port electrification options in exposure and adaptation models. It relates to the US ports EJSCREEN screening and the ICCT EU shore power study in the catalogue.
